title: Pick & Roll Basics
description: The most important two-man action in basketball: one player screens for the ball handler, then rolls or pops.
whatIsIt: The pick-and-roll (PNR) is a two-player action: one offensive player sets a screen (the pick) for the ball handler, and then moves toward the basket (the roll) or out to space (the pop). It is the most-run action in modern basketball at every level.

What makes it special is the math. The screen momentarily takes one defender out of the play, creating a two-on-one: ball handler and screener against the ball handler's defender and the screener's defender. If both offensive players read correctly, the defense cannot guard both.
Every advanced concept — Spain PNR, short rolls, snake dribbles — is just a variation on these basics. Master the foundation and the rest becomes readable.
whyItMatters: Pick-and-roll is the backbone of modern offense because it manufactures an advantage from nothing. Even without a great one-on-one player, a well-run PNR forces the defense to make a decision — and every decision leaves something open. Teams that run it well score efficiently; teams that defend it poorly give up layups and open threes all game.

howTo.title: Set the screen at the right spot
howTo.detail: The screener sprints to set the screen on the ball handler's defender, usually at the top or on the wing. Feet wide, knees bent, completely still — moving screens are turnovers.

howTo.title: Angle the screen
howTo.detail: The screener's chest should face the defender's path, steering the ball handler toward the middle or the sideline depending on the game plan.

howTo.title: Wait for contact
howTo.detail: The ball handler must be patient — let the defender run into the screen. Going too early wastes the pick and lets the defender slide under.

howTo.title: Go shoulder-to-shoulder
howTo.detail: The ball handler dribbles tight off the screener's hip, forcing the on-ball defender to go over or under. A wide turn gives the defender room to recover.

howTo.title: Read the two defenders
howTo.detail: After the screen, read: did the on-ball defender go over, under, or get stuck? Did the screener's defender drop, hedge, or switch? The answer tells you whether to shoot, drive, or pass.

howTo.title: Screener: roll or pop
howTo.detail: If the screener's defender helps on the ball, roll hard to the rim. If that defender stays back or the screener can shoot, pop out to space for a jumper.

coachingPoints: Teach patience first — young players rush the screen and never create real separation.
The screener should call out the screen and point the ball handler toward the open side.
Reps at game speed: walk-through PNR teaches nothing about timing and contact.
Start 2v2 before adding help defenders; let players master the two-on-one read.
commonMistakes: Slipping the screen every time instead of making contact — no contact, no advantage.
The ball handler dribbling away from the screen or too wide around it.
The screener rolling to a spot where their own defender is already waiting.
Both players looking at each other instead of reading the defense.
gameSituations: Against any man-to-man defense as a primary half-court weapon.
When you have a guard who can shoot or a big who can finish — the classic PNR pairing.
Late-clock: one good screen is often enough to create a shot.
